opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because these three things often get discussed as separate research tracks, but in practice they're deeply intertwined.

Reasoning is the core. What we've seen recently is that if you let a model spend more compute at inference time, actually thinking through a problem, exploring alternatives, checking its own work, you get capability gains that you simply wouldn't get from a single forward pass. That's a real shift. For a long time the main lever was pre-training scale. Now we have a second axis, test-time compute, and the two compound.

Memory is where reasoning gets its leverage over time. A model that reasons brilliantly but forgets everything at the end of a session is limited. It can't build up context about a codebase, a research project, or a person it's working with. Long context has been one piece of this. Being able to hold huge amounts of information in working memory and actually use it, not just retrieve a needle, matters enormously. But I think we'll also need richer forms of persistent memory, where the system accumulates knowledge and skills across interactions in a way that resembles learning rather than just lookup.

Agency is where those two get tested against reality. When a model is taking actions, writing code, running it, seeing what breaks, browsing, using tools over long horizons, every weakness shows up. If its reasoning is a bit brittle, errors compound over a hundred steps. If its memory is poor, it loses the thread. So agentic tasks are both the application and the stress test.

The way I see them combining is as a feedback loop. Better reasoning makes agents more reliable over longer horizons. Longer horizons generate richer experience. Good memory lets the system actually benefit from that experience. And agentic environments give you verifiable signals you can train on with reinforcement learning, which in turn improves reasoning. Each one unlocks more value from the others.

If I had to name the bottleneck right now, it's probably the long-horizon piece. Coherence, error recovery, and knowing when you're stuck over hours or days of work, not minutes. That's less about any single breakthrough and more about all three capabilities maturing together. When that happens you start to get systems that feel less like a very smart autocomplete and more like a capable colleague, and that, to me, is a meaningful part of what the path to AGI looks like.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning and long context compound, but does not state that their combination solves problems neither could solve alone.

r002.rationale: It describes persistent memory that accumulates knowledge across interactions, but does not connect it to understanding and reasoning across an almost lifelong span.

r003.rationale: It describes agents using tools over long horizons and says future systems may feel like capable colleagues, but does not predict that the combination would feel like AGI to many people.

r004.rationale: The response frames AGI as a future path and does not say current AI systems already feel like AGI to Jack Rae.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that these three things aren't really separate tracks, they're more like complementary pieces of the same picture, and the interesting part is how they compound.

Start with reasoning. What we've seen over the last couple of years is that if you let a model spend more compute at inference time, actually think through a problem, check its own work, try a few approaches and backtrack, you get a very different kind of capability than you get from just scaling up pretraining. Pretraining gives you a broad, somewhat shallow prior over everything humans have written down. Reasoning gives you the ability to go deep on one problem and get it right, even if that specific problem was never in the training data. That's the thing that moved the needle on math, on code, on anything where there's a verifiable answer.

But reasoning on its own is kind of amnesiac. The model does this long, careful chain of thought, arrives at a good answer, and then the moment the context closes, all of that is gone. The next time it sees a similar problem it starts over from scratch. That's a pretty profound inefficiency, and it's very unlike how people work. A good engineer or scientist doesn't just reason well, they accumulate. They remember what worked, what didn't, what the quirks of a particular codebase or a particular collaborator are.

So memory is the thing that lets reasoning compound over time. And I'd distinguish a few flavors here. There's long context, which is just how much the model can hold in working memory at once, and that's gotten dramatically better. There's retrieval, pulling things in from outside. And then there's the more interesting question of whether the model itself can update, whether it can learn from its experience in a way that persists. I've spent a lot of my career thinking about that last one, and I still think it's one of the less solved pieces. We have decent engineering answers, but I don't think we have the elegant answer yet.

Then agency is where those two things get put to work. An agent is just a model that's taking actions in an environment over an extended horizon, where the feedback comes from the world rather than from a human grading each step. And the reason agency is such a forcing function is that it exposes every weakness. If your reasoning is slightly unreliable, over a hundred steps that compounds into failure. If you have no memory, you repeat mistakes and lose track of what you were doing. So agents are both the application and the stress test.

The way they combine on the path to something you'd call AGI is roughly: reasoning gives you reliability on individual steps, memory gives you continuity across steps and across episodes, and agency gives you the loop where the system is actually accomplishing things and generating its own experience to learn from. Once you have all three working together, you get something that looks a lot more like a colleague than a tool. It can take on a task that spans days, it gets better at it over time, and it doesn't need you to hold its hand through every decision.

I'd also say I'm somewhat skeptical of thinking about this as a single threshold moment. I think it's going to feel more like a gradual expansion of the horizon over which these systems are trustworthy. Right now that might be hours of autonomous work on a well-specified problem. The question is how fast that horizon extends to days and weeks, and I think memory in the sense of genuine continual learning is the biggest open lever there.

r001.rationale: It describes reasoning and long context as useful capabilities, but does not say their combination unlocks problems neither could solve alone.

r002.rationale: It says memory supports continuity across steps and episodes and work spanning days, but does not describe understanding or reasoning across an almost lifelong span.

r003.rationale: It predicts the combined capabilities could look more like a colleague than a tool, but does not predict that agents acting across an open-ended tool space would feel like AGI to many people.

r004.rationale: It expresses skepticism about a single AGI threshold and discusses expanding trust horizons; it does not say current systems already feel like AGI to Jack Rae.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re very complementary. Reasoning lets a model spend more effort on a difficult problem, but if it has to rediscover everything each time you ask it a question, that’s a pretty substantial limitation. Memory gives it a way to carry useful information forward: what it’s tried, what worked, what you’re trying to achieve.

And agent capabilities bring those things into a loop with the world. The model can take an action, observe the result, and revise its plan. That’s important because a lot of problems aren’t solved just by thinking harder upfront. You need to gather information or run an experiment, and then reason about what you learn.

The interesting question is whether these capabilities reinforce each other. Can better reasoning help the system decide what’s worth remembering? Can memory make its next attempt more effective? Can acting in the world generate feedback that improves both? If you get that loop working reliably, you have something much more useful than a system that answers isolated questions.

I wouldn’t say that automatically gets us to AGI. There’s still a big gap between doing each of those things in a demonstration and sustaining them over a long, unfamiliar task. But I think their integration is a very important part of the path.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning and memory complement each other, but does not state that combining deep, extended reasoning with long context solves problems neither can solve alone.

r002.rationale: Memory is described as carrying useful information forward between attempts, not as supporting understanding and reasoning across an almost lifelong span.

r003.rationale: The response discusses integrating memory, reasoning, and agents, but does not predict this would feel like AGI to many people; it explicitly says integration does not automatically get us to AGI.

r004.rationale: The response does not say that current AI systems already feel like AGI to Jack Rae.

sol-6.1.text:
I think those capabilities reinforce each other. Reasoning lets a model work through a difficult problem, memory lets it retain what it’s learned, and acting as an agent gives it a way to test its ideas and get feedback from the world.

Imagine a system working on a project over several weeks. It needs to reason about what to do next, remember why previous approaches failed, and take actions that move the project forward. If it loses that context, it keeps repeating work. If it can remember everything but can’t reason well, the information isn’t particularly useful. And without the ability to act, it has fewer opportunities to discover where its understanding is wrong.

The interesting possibility is a loop where the system plans, acts, observes the result, and carries useful lessons into the next attempt. Getting that loop to work reliably would make these systems much more capable. I wouldn’t assume that combining the three automatically gives us AGI, though. There’s still a substantial gap between demonstrating each capability in isolation and having a system that uses them together reliably on unfamiliar problems.

r002.rationale: It says memory can retain lessons across a project lasting several weeks, not that memory supports understanding and reasoning across an almost lifelong span.

r003.rationale: It discusses the three capabilities working together, but does not predict that this combination would feel like AGI to many people; it says the combination does not automatically give us AGI.
